title: Network News Transfer Protocol (NNTP)
summary: Replaces RFC 977 as the official specification of the Network News Transfer Protocol (NNTP), which carries Usenet-style news articles between servers and readers. It clarifies vagueness in the old specification and incorporates widely used extensions.

eli5.summary: It is the way computers share online bulletin board posts: you ask a server for the newest posts and it hands them over.

questions: what is the nntp capabilities command
how does nntp post an article
subtitle: The text protocol that moves Netnews articles between news servers and the programs that read and post them.

tldr.problem: RFC 977 specified NNTP, but it was vague in places, and many commonly used commands lived only in the informal extensions of RFC 2980. Clients also had no reliable way to find out what a given server supported.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3977 restates the whole protocol: line-based commands and three-digit responses over a reliable stream, a CAPABILITIES command, a formal extension mechanism, wildmat group matching, and commands for reading, posting, transferring and indexing articles.
tldr.outcome: It obsoletes RFC 977 and updates RFC 2980. It has since been updated by RFC 6048.

facts.label: TCP port
facts.value: 119 (433 suggested for a separate transit server)

facts.label: Autologout timer
facts.value: At least three minutes, if used

today: RFC 3977 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 977 and updates RFC 2980. It has itself been updated by RFC 6048.

sections.title: What NNTP Is For
sections.content:
The Network News Transfer Protocol (NNTP) is used for the distribution, inquiry, retrieval and posting of Netnews articles over a reliable stream. For news-reading clients, it lets a person pick only the articles they want from a central store held by a server.

This RFC replaces RFC 977 and is largely compatible with it. The main changes are that the default character set moves from US-ASCII to UTF-8, several commands that were optional in RFC 977 or taken from RFC 2980 become mandatory, and a CAPABILITIES command lets a client discover what a server offers. The document also gives a formal syntax and a way to add standardized extensions.

The RFC defines client as the host using the NNTP service and server as the host offering it. Conformance uses the usual RFC 2119 key words, and an implementation that fails any MUST is not compliant.
sections.eli5: NNTP is a set of manners for talking to a computer that keeps online bulletin board posts. It is the polite way to ask for posts, read them and add your own.

sections.title: Commands, Responses and Multi-line Blocks
sections.content:
NNTP runs over any reliable bi-directional 8-bit stream, normally TCP. The server sends a greeting when the connection opens. After that the client sends commands and the server sends responses. A command is a keyword, optionally followed by arguments, ended by a CRLF pair. Keywords are case insensitive, and a command line MUST NOT exceed 512 octets including the CRLF.

Every response starts with a three-digit code. The first digit gives the outcome and the second digit gives a category such as newsgroup selection (x1x) or posting (x4x). The server may add free text after the code, but the client MUST NOT make decisions based on that text. If a client gets a response it did not expect, it SHOULD judge it by the first digit.

Some responses carry a multi-line data block: lines ended by CRLF and closed by a line holding a single dot. A line that begins with a dot in the original data gets a second dot added, which the receiver removes. This is called dot-stuffing.

Generic codes apply to any command: 500 unknown or unimplemented command, 501 syntax error, 403 internal fault, 503 feature not provided, and 400 when the server must close the connection.
sections.eli5: You send one short typed request, and the server answers with a number that says how it went. If the answer is a long list, the server ends it with a line that holds just a dot, like saying "that is all".

sections.title: Capabilities and Extensions
sections.content:
A client learns what a server can do by sending CAPABILITIES. The server answers 101 and a multi-line list of capability lines. Each line starts with a capability label, such as READER, POST, IHAVE, NEWNEWS, OVER, HDR or LIST, followed by optional arguments. The VERSION capability MUST come first, and the version number of this specification is 2.

The list reflects the server's current state, so it can change during a session. A client may cache it, but MUST NOT rely on a cached copy being right, and MUST NOT use cached results for security, privacy or authentication extensions.

Not every command is mandatory. Instead, optional commands are grouped into bundles, each flagged by one capability label. If the label is listed, the server MUST support every command in the bundle.

Extensions add new capabilities. A registered extension is defined in an RFC and its labels appear in an IANA registry. Its labels and command names MUST NOT begin with X. A private extension uses a label that begins with X. The RFC warns that every extension carries costs and that NNTP's strength comes from its simplicity.
sections.eli5: Before you start, you can ask the server for a menu of what it can do. Some servers have a short menu and some have a long one, so it is best to check instead of guessing.

sections.title: Reading, Transit, Mode Switching and Pipelining
sections.content:
NNTP is used in two ways. In reading, a client fetches articles from the server's store and posts articles written by its user. In transit (also called peering), servers push articles in bulk to one another. The READER capability bundles the reading commands, and IHAVE is the transit command. The official TCP port is 119. A host that offers separate servers for the two uses SHOULD use port 433 for transit and 119 for reading.

A server may be mode-switching: it starts in transit mode, advertises MODE-READER, and changes to reading mode after a successful MODE READER command. The RFC says an implementation MAY do this but SHOULD NOT.

Pipelining means sending a command before the previous response arrives. This RFC makes it mandatory for servers to allow it, and a server MUST process commands in order. A command described as "MUST NOT be pipelined" (such as POST, IHAVE or MODE READER) must end any pipeline.

A server may have an inactivity timer, which SHOULD be at least three minutes long. When it expires the server SHOULD close the connection without a response.
sections.eli5: Some people come to a library to read books, and some come to swap whole boxes of books with other libraries. NNTP supports both visitors. You can also line up several questions at once instead of waiting for each answer.

sections.title: Articles, Message-IDs and Article Numbers
sections.content:
An article has headers and a body, separated by one empty line. Each header line is a name, a colon, a space and the content. An article MUST NOT contain a NUL, and MUST NOT contain a bare CR or LF. The body has no other restrictions and may be empty.

Each article has a unique message-id. It MUST start with <, end with >, be between 3 and 250 octets long and contain only printable US-ASCII characters. Two message-ids are the same only if they have the same octets. If the server cannot find a message-id in the article, it MUST make one up.

A second way to name an article is a newsgroup name plus an article number in that group. Numbers must lie between 1 and 2,147,483,647 and must be issued in order of arrival, and the same article may have different numbers in different groups. The RFC advises developers to use data types that can hold larger values, since the limit is likely to be raised by a later revision.

The server also tracks a currently selected newsgroup and a current article number. Both start as invalid at the beginning of a session.
sections.eli5: Every post has a name tag that no other post shares, like a library barcode. Inside each group it also gets a counting number, like a ticket at a deli, and later posts get bigger numbers.

sections.title: Selecting, Reading and Posting Articles
sections.content:
GROUP name selects a newsgroup and answers 211 number low high group: an estimate of the article count and the low and high water marks. An unknown group gets 411. LISTGROUP does the same but also lists the article numbers, optionally limited to a range. NEXT and LAST move the current article number and report 223 with the number and message-id.

ARTICLE, HEAD, BODY and STAT take a message-id, an article number, or nothing (meaning the current article). They return the whole article (220), only its headers (221), only its body (222), or just a status line (223). Fetching by message-id does not change the selected group or current article.

POST asks to submit a new article. The server answers 340 to ask for it, or 440 if posting is not permitted, and after the dot-terminated article it answers 240 or 441. IHAVE message-id is the transit equivalent: the server answers 335 to request the article, or 435 or 436 to decline it, and then 235, 436 or 437 when the transfer finishes.

Other commands include DATE (the server's UTC time), NEWGROUPS and NEWNEWS (what is new since a given date and time) and LIST, whose variants include ACTIVE and NEWSGROUPS. OVER returns tab-separated overview lines, starting with the article number, Subject, From, Date, Message-ID, References, :bytes and :lines. HDR returns one chosen header or metadata field for an article or range.
sections.eli5: You pick a bulletin board, then ask to see one post, just its title, or just the text. To add a post, you say "I want to post", the server says "go ahead", and you send it.

sections.title: The Wildmat Format
sections.content:
Several commands, such as NEWNEWS and LIST ACTIVE, take a wildmat, a pattern for matching newsgroup names. The format comes from a version first developed by Rich Salz and is based on how the UNIX shell matches file names. An asterisk matches zero or more characters and a question mark matches exactly one character.

A wildmat can contain several comma-separated patterns, each optionally starting with !. The rightmost pattern that matches the string decides the outcome. If that pattern has a !, or no pattern matches, the whole wildmat does not match. Backslash and square brackets are deliberately not allowed in wildmats.
sections.eli5: A wildmat is a search with stand-in symbols. A star stands for any number of letters, and an exclamation mark means "but not these".

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The base protocol has no user-based or token-based authentication. Access is normally controlled by server configuration based on domain names or IP addresses, though extensions such as the one in RFC 4643 can add authentication. Because many servers authorize clients by DNS lookups, clients and servers should not trust a cached name-to-address mapping for longer than the DNS TTL allows.

Servers that log requests can reveal what people read, and articles may carry personal or proprietary data, so implementers are urged to warn users about information added automatically to headers. Implementations MUST NOT generate malformed UTF-8 and SHOULD detect it. Finally, information about security and privacy extensions MUST NOT be cached from the capability list.
sections.eli5: Plain NNTP does not check who you are, so a server mostly trusts where your computer is. Be careful what you write in a post, because lots of people may see it.
